endorsements.quote: (3) assign a named owner responsible for monitoring outputs, retesting after model updates, and retiring the tool if quality degrades;
(4) establish accountability for AI-generated error—the supervising educator, not the model, remains responsible for what learners are exposed to;

(1) define what data must never be entered into a public platform (real patient identifiers, uploaded clinical records, and any institution confidential material) and state this rule to learners in writing;
(2) verify the platform’s data retention and training settings and prefer institutionally licensed tools with enterprise privacy terms where available;
(5) train learners explicitly to interrogate AI outputs rather than accept them.
Pilot-testing should include structured review by a subject matter expert assessing content accuracy across a range of likely learner inputs.
In the Depression Avatars project, psychiatric experts reviewed AI-generated patient profiles and scripts before student exposure to ensure clinical accuracy and cultural appropriateness.

Ongoing monitoring of chatbot outputs is essential: AI systems evolve with platform updates, and a chatbot that performed appropriately at launch may require re-evaluation following changes to the underlying model.

Learners should be clearly informed that they are interacting with an AI tool, that its outputs may contain inaccuracies, and that professional decision-making must always be grounded in verified evidence and supervised practice.

This grounds the chatbot’s responses in curriculum-specific content rather than generic model outputs and enables alignment between chatbot feedback and formal assessment criteria.

Common failure modes to anticipate and test for include excessive unprompted disclosure of information, inaccurate disciplinary content, feedback that is too vague or poorly anchored to learning objectives, and persona inconsistency across extended interactions.
Educators should attend to demographic and cultural biases embedded in the underlying LLM that may produce personas or scenarios that are unrepresentative or culturally insensitive.

unlisted_practices: Embed safety messaging in the chatbot system prompt instructing it to acknowledge uncertainty and direct users to trusted clinical references.
Do not use no-code chatbots for high-stakes summative assessment.
Do not enter patient-identifiable or confidential data into consumer chatbot platforms.
Secure institutional support, licensing, and data governance approval before deploying educational chatbots.
Test chatbot outputs after each knowledge document upload to verify the material influences responses appropriately.
Situate educational chatbots within a planned curriculum sequence as a supplement to, not a replacement for, authentic experience.
